title: Mishneh Torah
hookLine: a fourteen-book code of all Jewish law in clear Hebrew

lines: A KING'S COPY OF THE LAW.
THE CODE THAT HOLDS IT ALL.
cards: A king of Israel, the Torah says, must write for himself "a copy of this law" and keep it with him, reading it all the days of his life. In Hebrew, that copy is called mishneh torah.
Maimonides took those two words for the name of his code of law. The laws of character from the last two days, the middle way and the far side of anger and pride, come from it. Today, the whole book.

teach.b: Mishneh Torah. Maimonides explains the name himself, in his introduction.

A person reads the written Torah first, he says, and then reads this book, and from it knows the whole oral law, without needing any other book in between. That's a bold aim, and he says it plainly. First, the language.
His commentary on the Mishnah was in Arabic.

This time he writes in Hebrew, in the clear Hebrew of the Mishnah, short and direct, so the law can be read without a long argument attached. Second, the order. The Talmud follows its conversations wherever they wander.
Maimonides sorts the law by subject instead: prayer with prayer, Shabbat with Shabbat, damages with damages.

teach.h: SORTED BY SUBJECT, IN FOURTEEN BOOKS.
teach.b: He divides it into fourteen books, each with its own sections. Third, the reach. He includes everything, even laws no one could keep in his day: the Temple service, the kings, the sacrifices.
The whole law, as if it might all be needed again. Fourth, the cost. Because he gives rulings without naming his sources, some rabbis objected.
One of them, the Ra'avad, wrote sharp notes against him, and in printed editions those notes sit right beside the text.

teach.h: THE CRITIC ON THE SAME PAGE.
teach.b: The code and its critic share the page. This path has met that pattern before: a book of law, and an answer printed next to it. Still, a reader who opens it finds the law laid out from the first page to the last.

how: The Mishneh Torah is studied in yeshivas and in daily study programs that read it in order, and rabbis consult it alongside later codes; printed editions carry the Ra'avad's critical notes and later commentaries beside the text.

games.q: you're Maimonides, writing a code of all Jewish law. how do you arrange it?
o: follow the Talmud's order, conversation by conversation.
sort it by subject, with each topic in its own place.
games.why: he sorts the law by subject into fourteen books, so a reader can find each topic in one place.

practice: Picture a shelf where everything you need is in its place, one subject beside the next, and notice how the body feels when things have an order.
Then pick one subject from your own life you'd like to understand better: Shabbat, prayer, charity, food. Rest in that order for a few breaths.

wordCard.voice: Mishneh Torah. Maimonides' code of Jewish law, in clear Hebrew, sorted by subject into fourteen books, named for the king's copy of the law. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole law in order. And a critic printed right beside it. Until tomorrow.
